title: Computer Application in Business

pattern.summary: 8 questions, attempt any 5, each carries 20 marks. Mostly theory with many 'compare' and 'short notes' questions; a few questions on ratios, NPV/IRR and depreciation.

choosing: Cyber security (CIA principles, authentication vs authorisation, CAPTCHA, GDPR) appears in every paper — the most reliable topic.
'Compare' and 'short notes' questions (4–5 parts × 4–5 marks) reward broad revision: learn one-line differences for every pair in the Key points.
Mail merge, operating systems and e-payment methods are asked most sessions.
numerical: For ratios, write the formula, then an example with figures, then what a high or low value means.
For NPV/IRR, show the Excel syntax: =NPV(rate, value1, …) + initial outlay, and =IRR(values).

topics.name: Cyber Security, Authentication & Data Protection
topics.summary: CIA principles, authentication vs authorisation, 2FA and OTP, CAPTCHA, identity theft, firewall, GDPR vs DPD.
points: IT security protects confidentiality (only authorised access), integrity (data not altered) and availability (usable when needed).
The book's key principles: identification (user states who they are), authentication (identity checked against stored data) and authorisation (what the user may access).
Security actions for a business include a firewall, antivirus software, complex passwords, regular backup, penetration testing and limiting access to critical data.
Cryptography protects data; an electronic (digital) signature confirms who sent a message and that it is genuine.
Identity theft: stealing personal details (card, Aadhaar, passwords) to commit fraud.
CAPTCHA ('Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart', 2003) keeps bots out of forms and logins. Types: text, image, audio, mathematical, logic and gamification.
OTP (one-time password): a code valid for one login or transaction, sent to the registered mobile or made by a token; with the normal password it gives two-factor authentication.

GDPR replaced the EU Data Protection Directive (DPD, 95/46/EC). It widens 'personal data' (biometric, genetic, economic identity), gives the right to access data and to be forgotten, makes data processors as well as controllers responsible, and requires 'privacy by design' with stiff penalties.
topics.frame: Definition → principles with one example each → a comparison table where asked → conclusion.
examples:
Example: identification, authentication and authorisation at a bank website
A customer types their customer ID (identification), enters the password and then an OTP sent to their registered mobile (authentication — two factors: something they know and something they have). Once inside, they can see only their own accounts and transfer up to their set limit (authorisation).

Example: identity theft by phishing
An SMS says 'Your KYC will expire — update now' with a link to a fake bank page. The victim enters card details and the OTP, and money is withdrawn. Safeguards: never share OTPs or PINs, check the website address, and use the bank's own app.

topics.name: Software & Operating Systems
topics.summary: System vs application software, OS functions and types, language processors, utility programs, open source.
points: Software is of two types: system software runs the hardware (operating system, drivers, utilities); application software does user tasks (Word, Excel, Tally, SPSS, Photoshop).
Operating system: manages hardware and gives services to programs. Functions: process, memory, file, device and security management, and the user interface.
Types of OS: batch, time-sharing, real-time, distributed, network, desktop (Windows, Linux) and mobile (Android, iOS).
Windows is a proprietary graphical OS used on desktops and laptops; Android is an open-source, Linux-based mobile OS now also used on wearables, TVs and consoles.
Google Play Store is Android's digital store for downloading apps.
Language processors: compiler (translates the whole program at once), interpreter (line by line, easier to debug), assembler (assembly language to machine code).
Utility programs maintain the system: antivirus, disk clean-up, backup, compression, defragmenter.
Free and open-source software: the source code can be used, changed and shared (Linux, LibreOffice).
topics.frame: Definition → functions or types as headed points → comparison table → examples.
examples:
Examples: which kind of software?
Windows 11 and Android → system software (operating systems). A printer driver and an antivirus → system software (driver and utility). Tally, MS Excel and Photoshop → application software. LibreOffice and Linux → free and open-source software.

Example: compiler vs interpreter
A C program is compiled — the whole program is translated into machine code first, and errors are reported together. A Python program is interpreted — run line by line, stopping at the first error, which makes debugging easier.

topics.name: Networks, Internet & E-mail
topics.summary: Network types, internet vs intranet vs extranet, WWW, URLs and domains, browsers, e-mail protocols, cloud computing.
points: A computer network is a chain of nodes linked by communication channels that share data, programs and databases.
Types by area: PAN (one person, about 10 m), LAN (one building), MAN (a town, city or campus — several LANs), WAN (a country or continents; the internet is a public WAN) and HAN (a home).
Internet: a global network of networks working on common protocols. Intranet: a private network inside one organisation. Extranet: part of an intranet opened to partners.
Internet services: e-mail, World Wide Web, web services, FTP (file transfer), chat rooms, mailing lists and newsgroups.
The WWW is a service on the internet (linked web pages); the internet is the network itself. A web browser lets you view hypertext pages — graphical (Chrome) or non-graphical (text only).
E-mail protocols: SMTP sends mail; POP3 downloads mail to one device (usually removing it from the server); IMAP keeps mail on the server and syncs across devices.
URL: the address of a web page. A domain name (e.g. ignou.ac.in) is a memorable shortcut for an IP address; DNS translates names into IP addresses.
Top-level domains: gTLD (generic — .com, .org) and ccTLD (country code — .in, .uk).
Cloud computing: using remote internet servers to store, manage and process data instead of a local computer; providers charge by use (Google Drive).
topics.frame: Definition → types in a table (range, example) → comparisons → conclusion.
examples:
Examples: which network?
Phone connected to a smartwatch by Bluetooth → PAN. Computers in one office connected to a shared printer → LAN. A college's buildings across a city connected together → MAN. A bank linking its branches across India → WAN. The staff-only portal of a company → intranet; opening part of it to suppliers → extranet.

Example: reading a URL and choosing an e-mail protocol
In https://www.example.com/courses/index.html — 'https' is the protocol, 'www.example.com' the domain name (.com is a generic top-level domain), and '/courses/index.html' the path to the page. DNS turns the domain name into the server's IP address.
Someone who reads mail on a phone and a laptop should use IMAP, so both show the same mailbox. With POP3, mail downloaded to one device may disappear from the other.

topics.name: MS Word, PowerPoint & Google Docs
topics.summary: Mail merge, word processing features, equation editor, presentations and animation, Google Docs vs Word.
points: Word processing: creating, editing, formatting, storing and printing documents; packages include MS Word, WordStar, WordPerfect and Google Docs.
MS Word 2010 tabs: File, Insert, Page Layout, References, Mailings, Review and View. Views: Print Layout, Full Screen Reading, Web Layout, Outline and Draft.
Editing and formatting: copy, undo/redo, find and replace, fonts, line spacing, borders and shading, bullets, indenting, margins, header and footer, tables, spell check, WordArt and SmartArt.
Mail merge (Mailings tab) makes many personalised copies: create the main document → create the data source → insert merge fields → merge.
Equation editor (Insert tab) inserts ready or custom equations; Track Changes (Review tab) records edits for review.
Referencing tools: footnote/endnote, index, table of contents, bookmark (named place to jump to), cross-reference, citation, placeholder and bibliography.
Google Docs is free, web-based and saves to the cloud so others can edit at once; Word files live on your computer unless shared.
PowerPoint: insert a slide from Home → New Slide, Ctrl+M, or right-click → New Slide; add graphs, diagrams, pictures, sound and video; save to external memory or the cloud.
topics.frame: Meaning → steps as a numbered list with menu paths → uses in business → conclusion.
examples:
Example: mail merge for 200 invitation letters
Write the main letter once in Word. Create the data source — an Excel sheet with Name, Address and City for 200 guests. Insert merge fields («Name», «Address») in the letter from the Mailings tab. Finish and merge to get 200 personalised letters, printed or e-mailed.

Example: a project report in Word
Use Heading styles for chapters and insert an automatic table of contents (References tab). Add footnotes for sources and a bibliography from the citations. Turn on Track Changes so the guide's corrections show up for you to accept or reject.

topics.name: Ratios, Capital Budgeting & Depreciation
topics.summary: Ratio analysis, NPV and IRR (with Excel syntax), depreciation methods, loan and lease statements, payroll.
points: Loan statement: prepared by the lender — loan amount, interest rate, period and instalments (Excel =PMT gives the EMI). Lease statement: the periodic payments by the lessee (tenant) to the lessor (owner).
Ratio analysis uses the trading account, profit and loss account and balance sheet to judge the firm's position.
Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities (2:1 is the usual norm). Quick ratio = quick assets ÷ current liabilities (1:1).
Gross profit ratio = GP ÷ net sales × 100; net profit ratio = NP ÷ net sales × 100; inventory turnover = cost of goods sold ÷ average inventory.
Payroll statement: employee name, code, category, basic pay, allowances and perquisites, deductions, tax and net salary.

Capital budgeting evaluates long-term projects by their cash inflows and outflows. NPV = present value of inflows − outlay (accept if positive); IRR is the rate at which NPV = 0 (accept if above the cost of capital).
In Excel: =NPV(rate, later cash flows) + the initial outlay (entered as negative); =IRR(range including the outlay).
Depreciation: straight line (same amount each year, =SLN) and diminishing balance (fixed % of the reducing balance, =DB).
mistakes: Forgetting that Excel's NPV() does not include the year-0 outlay.
examples:
Example: EMI with PMT
A loan of ₹1,00,000 at 10% a year, repaid monthly over 12 months:
=PMT(10%/12, 12, -100000) gives an EMI of ₹8,791.59.

Example: NPV and IRR in Excel
Outlay ₹1,00,000 in B1 (entered as −100000); inflows of ₹45,000 in B2:B4 for 3 years; cost of capital 10%.
=NPV(10%, B2:B4) + B1 = 1,11,908 − 1,00,000 = ₹11,908 → positive, so accept.
=IRR(B1:B4) ≈ 16.6%, above the 10% cost of capital.
Depreciation of a ₹1,00,000 asset, scrap ₹10,000, life 5 years: =SLN(100000, 10000, 5) = ₹18,000 a year.

topics.name: E-payment, Plastic Money & Wallets
topics.summary: E-payment methods, plastic money, NEFT vs RTGS, digital wallets, QR codes, B2B vs B2C.
points: Plastic money: credit, debit, smart, charge and stored-value cards, named after the plastic they are made of; money evolved from barter to coins, paper, cheques and cards.
E-payment: paying for goods and services electronically without cash or cheques.

Methods in the book: QR code (2-D barcode scanned to pay), UPI (virtual address, no account number needed), digital wallets, USSD (*99# on basic phones), MMID (7-digit mobile money ID), IMPS, AEPS (pay with Aadhaar), NFC, internet banking and cards.
E-wallet: a virtual wallet loaded with money from cards or bank for merchant payments and transfers.
Growth drivers: Digital India, demonetisation, cheap smartphones and data, better payment infrastructure and wallet promotions.
NEFT settles in batches; RTGS settles each payment in real time and is meant for large amounts (minimum ₹2 lakh).
Safety: never share OTP or PIN, use secure (https) sites, check merchant details, turn on alerts.
B2B e-commerce: business sells to business; B2C: business sells to consumers.
topics.frame: Meaning → methods as headed points → merits and precautions → conclusion.

units.title: Plastic Money, E-Wallets and Online Pay

examples:
Example: choosing a payment method
Paying a vegetable seller ₹60 → scan their QR code with a UPI app.
Sending ₹20,000 to a relative at night → IMPS or UPI, which work 24×7 and credit at once.
Paying a supplier ₹5 lakh → RTGS (for ₹2 lakh and above; settled individually in real time).
A farmer with a basic phone and no internet → dial *99# (USSD) to transfer money.

Example: B2B vs B2C
A textile mill ordering dyes from a chemical company's online portal → B2B. A student buying earphones on a shopping app → B2C.

topics.name: Business Information Systems (MIS, DSS, ERP)
topics.summary: Business and information systems, MIS vs DSS, ERP, data vs information, business ownership forms.
points: Data are raw facts; information is data processed into a meaningful form for decisions.
A business information system supports effective decision-making; key aspects are the business plan, market analysis, sales and funding, organisation management and financial projections.
Information systems divide into operation support systems (e.g. transaction processing) and management support systems (MIS, DSS).
MIS: a computerised database that stores the firm's (mainly financial) information and gives regular reports — e.g. bank, railway and inventory management systems.
DSS: analyses data and presents it so users can make decisions; works on 'decide – act – review'. Types: communication-, data-, document-, knowledge- and model-driven.

MIS vs DSS: primary vs highest decision level; reports vs analysis of choices; operational efficiency vs effective decisions; large volume of transaction data vs smaller filtered data; summary reports vs decision analysis.
ERP: integrates information between customer, vendor and manufacturer over networks; it evolved from MRP and MRP II.
Forms of business by ownership: sole proprietorship, partnership, company, cooperative.
topics.frame: Definition → block diagram (inputs → processing → outputs, with feedback) → types → importance for business.
examples:
Example: information systems in a supermarket chain
Every bill at the counter is recorded — a transaction processing (operation support) system.
The MIS turns these into a weekly report: sales by store and product, and stock below the reorder level.
The DSS lets the manager ask 'what if we give 10% off on biscuits next month?' and see the likely effect on sales and profit.
ERP links it all — sales, purchase, warehouse, suppliers and accounts — so a sale at one store updates stock and triggers a purchase order automatically.

topics.name: DBMS, RDBMS & Data Models
topics.summary: File processing vs DBMS, DBMS vs RDBMS, data models, data abstraction and independence, database administrator.
points: A DBMS is a collection of logically related data plus the operations needed to access it. A database system = database + DBMS.
Functions: define the structure and data types, add, update, delete and read data, keep it consistent, stop unauthorised access and allow recovery.
Limitations of file processing systems that a DBMS overcomes: data redundancy and inconsistency, data isolation, difficult access, integrity problems, concurrency problems and weak security.
Data models: record-based (hierarchical, network, relational) and object-based (entity–relationship, object-oriented). The relational model is the most widely used.
RDBMS stores data in tables (relations): row = tuple, column = attribute, schema = overall design, instance = the data at a given moment.

Data abstraction has three levels: physical (how data is stored), logical (what data is stored and how it relates) and external or view (what each user sees). Data independence lets one level change without affecting the next.
Database administrator (DBA): has overall control — designs the schema, grants access, handles backup and recovery.
topics.frame: Definition → diagram of the three levels → comparison table → conclusion.
examples:
Example: a relational table
Table STUDENT (the schema): Enrolment_No, Name, Course, City. Each row, such as (2301, Anu, BCom, Kochi), is a tuple; each column is an attribute. The rows stored today are the instance — they change as students join and leave; the schema does not.

Example: why a DBMS beats separate files
The fees office and the exam office each keep a file with the student's address. When a student moves, one file is updated and the other is not — redundancy leads to inconsistency. In a DBMS the address is stored once and both offices see the same data, with access controlled by the DBA.
Data independence: moving the database to a faster disk (physical level) does not change the tables users see.

topics.name: Computer Fundamentals & Generations
topics.summary: What a computer is, generations, types (analog/digital/hybrid, micro to super), hardware components, applications.
points: A computer is a programmable electronic device that does four things: accepts data (input), processes it, gives results (output) and stores them.
Hardware: input devices, CPU (ALU, control unit, registers), memory (RAM, ROM), storage and output devices. Software makes the hardware useful.

The book's six generations: 1st (1940–56) vacuum tubes and machine language; 2nd (1956–63) transistors; 3rd (1964–71) integrated circuits; 4th (1972–2010) microprocessors, networks and the internet; 5th (2010–20) parallel processing and AI; 6th (2020 on) nanotechnology.
Classification — by purpose: general or special purpose; by size and capacity: micro, mini, mainframe, super; by technology: analog (continuous data), digital (discrete) and hybrid (both).
Mainframes serve many users and huge transaction loads (banks); supercomputers are the fastest, used for scientific work such as weather forecasting.
Applications: business, education, banking, insurance, healthcare, defence, communication and personal use.
Advantages: speed, accuracy, multitasking, storage, data security. Disadvantages: fewer jobs, loss of privacy, viruses and cybercrime.
topics.frame: Definition with a block diagram (Input → CPU → Output, with memory) → classification table → applications.
examples:
Examples: classify the computer
A desktop in an office → general-purpose microcomputer. An ATM or a washing-machine controller → special-purpose. A bank's central system handling lakhs of transactions → mainframe. Weather forecasting → supercomputer. A hospital ICU machine that measures a patient's temperature and pulse (continuous) and shows them as numbers (digital) → hybrid.

Example: input, process, output, storage
In a billing counter: barcodes scanned (input) → prices looked up and totalled by the CPU (processing) → bill printed (output) → sale saved in the database (storage).

topics.name: YouTube, AdSense & Digitisation
topics.summary: YouTube channels and revenue, Google AdSense, digitisation's impact on business, AI.
points: Multimedia combines text, images, sound, animation and video; animation creates the illusion of movement from still images, and PowerPoint has built-in animation tools.
YouTube is a video-sharing site. To upload: sign in → click Upload → choose the video and privacy setting → manage the upload.
Creating a channel: sign in with a Google account → create channel → add name, logo and description → upload and customise.
Google AdSense (2003) places ads on websites and YouTube and pays the owner for clicks or views; it is free and easy to join, but has strict policies and earns little without traffic.
YouTube pays creators through the YouTube Partner Programme, which has minimum subscriber and watch-time conditions.
Digitisation: converting information and processes to digital form — faster service, lower cost, online markets and data-based decisions.
AI now automates animation and rendering of visual effects.
topics.frame: Meaning → steps or advantages as headed points → examples → conclusion.
examples:
Example: a teacher starts a YouTube channel
She signs in with a Google account, creates the channel 'Easy Accounts', adds a logo and description, and uploads short lessons, choosing 'Public' as the privacy setting.
Once the channel meets the YouTube Partner Programme conditions on subscribers and watch time, ads (through AdSense) can be shown on her videos and she earns a share of the ad revenue.

topics.name: DPR, Research Proposal & Data Analysis
topics.summary: Detailed project report, research proposal components, data collection, frequency distribution, correlation and regression.
points: A detailed project report (DPR) is the base document for investment, approval, planning and implementation of a project.

DPR structure in the book: title page; name, affiliation, date; acknowledgement; contents; abbreviations; executive summary; introduction; background; technical and financial analysis; recommended action plan; appendices.
Business presentations inform, educate, motivate and persuade; types: group, presentation aid, persuasive and informative.
A research proposal presentation covers title, abstract, literature review, objectives, research methodology, references and annexes.
Project presentation steps: analyse the audience → select the topic → define the objective → prepare the body → prepare the introduction and conclusion.
Excel's Data Analysis ToolPak gives frequency distribution, descriptive statistics (mean, median, mode, SD, range, variance), correlation, regression and hypothesis tests (t-tests, z-test).
Correlation measures the strength of a linear relationship between two variables; regression shows how the dependent variable relates to independent variables.
topics.frame: Meaning → components as a numbered list → conclusion.
examples:
Example: a DPR for a small bakery unit
Executive summary (the project in one page) → introduction and background (demand for bakery products in the town) → technical analysis (site, ovens, capacity, staff) → financial analysis (project cost ₹25 lakh, funding, projected sales and profit, break-even, loan repayment) → recommended action plan with a timeline → appendices (quotations, licences).

Example: Excel Data Analysis ToolPak
Marks of 60 students in column A → Data → Data Analysis → Descriptive Statistics gives the mean, median, mode, standard deviation and range in one table. Choosing Correlation with study hours in column B shows how strongly hours and marks move together.

topics.name: MS Excel Features & Functions
topics.summary: Charts, worksheets, relative vs absolute addressing, logical and financial functions, formulas vs functions.
points: A spreadsheet arranges data in rows and columns for organising and analysing, especially numbers. Excel screen: ribbon, quick access toolbar, title bar, formula bar, worksheet tabs.
Worksheets can be named, inserted, deleted, grouped, ungrouped, moved, hidden, linked and protected.
Addressing: relative (A1) changes when copied; absolute ($A$1) stays fixed; mixed ($A1 or A$1).
A formula is an expression of values, operators and cell references (=A1+B1). A function is a pre-defined formula: '=' + name + arguments (=SUM(A1:A10)).
Array formula (CSE — Ctrl+Shift+Enter) does many calculations on a range at once.
Function groups: statistical, financial, logical (IF, AND, OR), date and time, text (CONCATENATE), lookup (VLOOKUP, HLOOKUP) and math.
Charts make data readable; pivot tables and pivot charts summarise and cross-tabulate large data sets.
Sort and filter go together to prepare data; cell comments explain entries.
topics.frame: Meaning → syntax with an example formula → use in business → conclusion.
examples:
Example: relative and absolute references
Sales are in A3:A10 and the commission rate is in B1. In B3 type =A3*$B$1 and copy it down: A3 changes to A4, A5… (relative), but $B$1 stays fixed (absolute).

Example: useful functions
=SUM(C2:C31) totals a column. =IF(C2>=40,"Pass","Fail") marks each student. =VLOOKUP(102, A2:C50, 3, FALSE) finds item code 102 in the first column and returns its price from the third column. A pivot table then summarises sales by region and month in a few clicks.
